newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel wants lower taxes to spur investment, trade.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel wants lower taxes to spur investment, trade.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel outlined a tax reform proposal on Monday which he said were aimed at cutting taxes to stimulate investment, create jobs and make Germany more competitive globally.
He said he wanted the top income tax rate to fall to 35-40 percent from 53 percent now as the cornerstone of the plan.
The proposal was aimed at cutting the taxpayers' burden by 20-30 billion marks ($13-19.5 billion), he told a tax policy forum of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
Other countries have cut taxes in recent years, stimulating investment and creating millions of jobs, and Germany must follow suit if it is to remain competitive, Waigel said.
"We don't need more bureaucrats, we need more entrepreneurs, people who take risks. The symmetrical fiscal policy sets the right conditions," he said.
Waigel said tax policies must enhance the steps taken in the government's Programme for More Jobs and Growth.
The programme is proving politically unpopular. While most Germans see the need to cut government spending, they oppose the specific cuts the government has decided on.
"That is why we need strong political leadership," he said.
Waigel did not disclose the plan in full, arguing it would pre-empt the work of a commission he chairs and has until the end of 1996 to finish its task.
The Taxpayers' Alliance immediately criticised the proposal.

Deeper tax cuts of about 80 billion marks annually are needed to lure foreign investors and stimulate the economy, giving a supply-side push to the reform itself, said the alliance's president, Karl-Heinz Daeke.

The CDU must still hammer out its own party line. A CDU tax panel headed by Kohl's parliamentary lieutenant Wolfgang Schaueble seeks a cut in the top tax rate to 35 percent from 53 and a minimum rate to under 20 percent from 26 at present.
Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners, praised Waigel's plans but warned against a temptation to raise value-added tax to make up for shortfalls.
Even with lower tax rates, Germany still aims to drive its budget deficit far below the three percent of economic output demanded for participation in the single European currency.
Waigel said Germany will aim for a balanced budget in the future, making room for further tax cuts.
He said he aims to finance the reform by lowering government outlays, broadening the tax base and simplifying the system to reduce taxpayer deductions.
The reform would be implemented as planned in January 1999, despite pressure from the FDP and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to implement it sooner, he said.

Gross tax cuts would total between 80 and 90 billion marks on top of reductions in corporation and withholding taxes and a "solidarity" surcharge to help the former East Germany, that are already in the works, he said.
These gross reductions will be partly offset, however, by the closing of loopholes and simplification of deductions. ($1=1.5281 Mark)
